projects.title: GIS-Based Multi-Criteria Assessment of Hybrid Solar–Wind Suitability in Maharashtra
projects.summary: A district-level planning framework that maps where hybrid solar-wind projects make sense across all 36 districts of Maharashtra at 100 m resolution. It combines AHP-weighted resource and infrastructure criteria, 30 years of seasonal solar-wind complementarity, and pixel-level cost of energy, and it is validated against 292 operating plants (AUC 0.858).

meta.v: Maharashtra, India: 36 district
100 m pixels
GIS-based Analytic Hierarchy Process

sections.t: India’s electricity system faces three pressures at once: climate mitigation (the power sector produces about 40% of global CO₂ emissions), energy security (India imports about 85% of its crude oil), and rising demand (peak demand reached 250 GW in May 2024 and is projected to hit 458 GW by 2032). India targets 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and has about 283.5 GW installed. Maharashtra’s policy targets 100 GW by FY 2035–36 against about 31.7 GW today, so it must nearly triple capacity. Globally, solar and wind costs have fallen by about 90% and 70% since 2010, so the open question is where to build. The project names three gaps in existing studies: a spatial resolution gap (investment decisions are made on 1 km global data), commercial decoupling (maps show resources but not whether a site beats the grid tariff), and temporal neglect (January and July are treated as identical, though Maharashtra’s monsoon winds peak when solar output drops).

The objective is a reproducible GIS-AHP framework that maps solar-wind hybrid suitability across all 36 districts of Maharashtra at 100 m. It builds on a physical fact: summer solar and monsoon wind are naturally anti-correlated, so hybrid systems can smooth supply without storage. Three questions guide the work. Which districts show the highest hybrid suitability under a high-resolution multi-criteria framework? How is seasonal solar-wind complementarity distributed across the state, based on historical ERA5 data? Which zones are commercially viable when pixel-level LCOE is compared with grid tariffs?

Maharashtra spans 15.6°N–22.1°N and 72.6°E–80.9°E, covering 307,713 km² in western-central peninsular India. It has three physiographic zones. The Deccan Plateau is the primary hybrid zone, with excellent irradiance, gentle slopes and accessible infrastructure. The Western Ghats hold the state’s best wind resource but are constrained by the Forest Conservation Act and eco-sensitive regulations. The Konkan Coastal Strip is largely excluded because of steep slopes, forest cover and protected areas.

Solar: Global Solar Atlas v2.0 (GHI and PV output, 1999–2018). Wind: Global Wind Atlas v3.0 (wind speed at 100 m and IEC Class 2 capacity factor, 2000–2019). Terrain: SRTM 1 arc-second DEM (slope derived in QGIS). Land cover: ESA WorldCover. Protected areas: WDPA. Roads and power transmission lines: OpenStreetMap (2025, via Overpass Turbo). Climate complementarity: ERA5 monthly data, January 1993–December 2023. District boundaries: Survey of India (DataMeet). Validation: Global Energy Monitor’s Global Integrated Power Tracker (March 2026). Analysis used QGIS, Google Earth Engine, Python (Pandas, NumPy, Rasterio, GeoPandas, SciPy, scikit-learn), Microsoft Excel and a custom financial model.

Four tracks fed one integrated synthesis. Exclusion mapping removed unbuildable land using slope above 20°, restricted land use (forests, built-up areas, water bodies, wetlands, mangroves) and a 1,000 m buffer around protected areas. In total, 30.7% of the state was excluded before scoring. Multi-criteria weighting scored six criteria from 1 to 5 and weighted them by AHP pairwise comparison: solar GHI 0.27, wind speed 0.22, seasonal complementarity 0.22, slope 0.15, grid proximity 0.09 and road proximity 0.05. The consistency ratio was 0.017, well under the 0.10 threshold. Climate complementarity came from Spearman rank correlation of solar and wind across 360 monthly values per pixel. Techno-economic modelling estimated pixel-level solar and wind LCOE with CERC 2024 parameters and compared it with grid tariffs. Final scores were validated by ROC analysis, stress-tested for weight sensitivity with Cohen’s kappa, and aggregated by district.

Solar GHI scored 4.90 out of 5 and is nearly uniform across the Deccan, so it does not differentiate sites. Wind scored 1.81 and is the most variable criterion: high wind sits along the Western Ghats escarpment (Nashik, Dhule, Satara, Sangli, Kolhapur) while the interior plateau is mostly low. Terrain slope scored 4.62, and the 20° threshold removes only 2.6% of the state. Grid proximity (mean 3.43) and road proximity (3.38) are good across most of the state, with poor access in Gadchiroli and parts of Chandrapur. Seasonal complementarity averaged 3.61. Nandurbar and Dhule show excellent complementarity (solar and wind peak at opposite times), while Kolhapur, Sangli and Sindhudurg are poor because solar and wind peak together.

After excluding 30.7% of the state, 68.6% (211,116 km²) remains technically suitable. The final map classes are Very High 13.8% (42,486 km²), High 31.5% (96,838 km²), Moderate 9.4%, Low 13.9% and Excluded 30.7%. High and Very High combined cover 139,324 km², or 45.3% of Maharashtra. The ten highest-ranked districts by mean suitability score are Washim (3.278), Nashik (2.905), Nandurbar (2.878), Hingoli (2.798), Jalna (2.779), Buldhana (2.773), Beed (2.755), Dhule (2.743), Dharashiv (2.687) and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (2.435). Washim leads by combining flat terrain with high solar irradiance. The bottom five districts all score below 0.50 because forest, coastal and urban land is excluded.

Solar PV has a state mean LCOE of about ₹3.09/kWh against a grid tariff benchmark of ₹6–8/kWh, and no pixel in Maharashtra exceeds ₹6/kWh. Solar economics are uniformly good statewide, so solar investment should be targeted by grid capacity, land availability and social factors. Wind is far more variable. Zone A (under ₹4/kWh) is immediately viable without subsidy, mainly along the Western Ghats. Zone B (₹6–10/kWh) is viable only as co-located hybrid with solar, and Zone C (above ₹20/kWh) needs policy support or grid investment first. Competitive wind covers only about 20% of the state, but it is world-class where it exists.

The model was tested against 403 plant locations from the Global Integrated Power Tracker. After removing 111 points that fell in excluded zones, 292 operating plants remained (253 solar and 39 wind). The area under the ROC curve was 0.858, meaning the framework ranks an operating plant above a random low-suitability location 85.8% of the time. 72.8% of plants fall in High or Very High classes, and the mean score at plant locations was 2.76 against 1.40 for the background. A sensitivity analysis rebuilt the map with solar-emphasis, wind-emphasis and equal-weight scenarios. Cohen’s kappa agreement with the base map was 0.985 (solar), 0.926 (wind) and 0.970 (equal weights), all above the 0.80 threshold for strong agreement.

Four actions are proposed. First, establish Priority Hybrid Investment Zones in the top 10 districts (MEDA and the State Planning Department, immediately). Second, incentivise co-located projects that exploit the negative solar-wind correlation (MSEDCL and MNRE, requiring a policy notification). Third, set localised LCOE-based benchmark tariffs instead of a flat grid tariff (MERC and CERC, at the next tariff revision cycle). Fourth, fast-track grid reinforcement on bare or sparsely vegetated land (MSEDCL and MEDA, in parallel with tendering).

Limitations: 100 m resolution suits district planning but not turbine micro-siting or exact array boundaries, so a 10–30 m study is needed before ground-breaking. ERA5 data are monthly, so the model captures seasonal complementarity but not daily cycles, and it cannot say how much storage overnight supply would still need. Tribal settlements, Forest Rights Act claims and community land use are not mapped, and some high-suitability pixels in Vidarbha likely overlap with contested land. Future work: hourly ERA5 reanalysis and a social exclusion layer (1–2 years), LCOE projections to 2030 and 2035 and system-wide storage savings (2–4 years), and a National Hybrid Renewable Energy Atlas covering all Indian states.

The project offers a district-level hybrid atlas for Maharashtra at 100 m, a seasonal complementarity layer built from 30 years of ERA5 data, pixel-level LCOE using Indian cost parameters, and an open-source, reproducible method that other states can reuse. Its central message is that Maharashtra does not have a resource problem but a planning problem.

projects.title: Rapid flood impact assessment for Kolhapur using SAR and deep learning
projects.summary: Deep learning flood mapping of the July 2022 Panchganga floods in Kolhapur district, using Sentinel-1 SAR and Landsat-8. Flood extent is overlaid on land cover, population and transport networks to show who and what was exposed.

meta.v: July 2022 Panchganga River floods
Sentinel-1 SAR, 18 Jan 2022 (pre) vs 17 Jul 2022 (post)
Kolhapur Municipal Corporation: 5.49 lakh people, 124,194 households

sections.t: Kolhapur lies in the Panchganga basin, fed by the Bhogawati, Tulsi, Kumbhi, Kasari and Doodhganga rivers, close to the Western Ghats. Heavy orographic rainfall, dam releases from Radhanagari and Warna, siltation and riverbank encroachment make the district flood-prone. Major floods occurred in 2005, 2019 and 2022. In July 2022, sustained rain pushed the river past the danger mark and flooded Kolhapur city and the Shirol, Hatkanangale, Karveer and Gaganbawada talukas. Sugarcane, paddy and vegetable crops were hit, sanitation and drinking water were disrupted, and schools and halls became relief shelters. The study asks whether satellite data and deep learning can give a fast, repeatable picture of the flood’s impact on land, people and infrastructure.

The workflow had four steps, all run in ArcGIS Pro in WGS 84 / UTM Zone 43N. For flood mapping, Sentinel-1 GRD images (VV and VH, IW mode) were calibrated to sigma-naught, despeckled with the Refined Lee filter and terrain-corrected with the SRTM DEM. Esri’s pretrained Waterbody Extraction (SAR) model then extracted water from the pre- and post-flood scenes. Both outputs were converted to binary masks (water = 1), and the Change Detection Wizard in Categorical Change mode isolated pixels that went from non-water to water, with the flooded area tabulated in km². For land cover, the Land Cover Classification (Landsat 8) model was applied to cloud-masked Level-2 surface reflectance bands, and the area of each class was computed. The flood raster was then overlaid on the land cover map to get the flooded area per class. Finally, flood extent was combined with 2011 Census village data, population grids and road and rail layers to assess exposure.

The study used Sentinel-1 SAR GRD scenes from the ASF Vertex portal, taken before the flood on 18 January 2022 and after it on 17 July 2022. Land cover came from Landsat-8 OLI Level-2 surface reflectance at 30 m, and terrain correction used a 30 m SRTM DEM. Both analyses relied on Esri’s pretrained deep learning packages (.dlpk). Socio-economic data came from the 2011 Census of India, covering households, population, the share of main workers who are agricultural labourers, and settlement area. This was supported by population, administrative boundary, built-up, road and rail layers, along with IMD rainfall records. The date of 17 July 2022 was chosen because it had the most complete and consistent rainfall data, not because it was the wettest day, and it fell within a week of heavy monsoon rain.

Open Water showed the most flooding in absolute terms, with 4.02 km² of its 9.54 km² affected (about 42%). Shrub/Scrub lost 3.15 km² and Herbaceous 2.30 km², while Developed Open Space lost 1.52 km² of 79 km² and Evergreen Forest 0.44 km². Wetland classes are small but proportionally exposed, whereas cropland and high- and medium-intensity built-up areas showed very little flooding.

Kolhapur Municipal Corporation dominates population exposure, with 549,236 people and 124,194 households, followed in household numbers by Shiroli, Uchgaon, Mudsingi, Rukadi and Wadange. Livelihood vulnerability follows a different pattern: rural villages show high agricultural-labour dependence, led by Wasagade (42.6%), Pimple T. Satave (36.7%) and Mauje Vadgaon (32.5%), with Rukadi, Nigave Dumala and Herle near 26–28%, while the cities sit under 1%. The report reads this as urban areas facing infrastructure and scale pressure, and rural areas facing loss of wages and assets.

NH 48, NH 166, NH 166H and the Miraj–Kolhapur railway all cross flooded areas, which put supply chains and emergency response at risk. The report concludes that deep learning-based geospatial assessment is a rapid, flexible way to support flood-zone regulation, crop insurance, resilient infrastructure design, relief planning and early warning.

projects.title: Land cover and spectral index mapping of Dhanbad’s coal-mining district
projects.summary: Maximum Likelihood land cover classification of Dhanbad district from Landsat 8, with NDVI and Bare Soil Index maps. The classification reached 91.4% overall accuracy and shows how much of the district is mined, barren or degraded.

meta.v: Dhanbad district, Jharkhand
Landsat 8 OLI Level-2 surface reflectance, 30 m, 3% cloud cover
Maximum Likelihood

sections.t: Dhanbad sits on the Chota Nagpur Plateau in the Damodar basin and is an intensively mined landscape. Forest remnants, farmland, dense settlements, scattered water bodies and open-cast coalfield land (the Jharia coalfield) all sit close together. Deforestation, land degradation and periodic drought add to the pressure. The project asks how well freely available satellite data and open-source tools can map this mix. It also asks which parts of the district show vegetation stress or exposed soil, which are the places that matter for restoration and disaster-risk planning.

All work was done in QGIS 3.34 with the Semi-Automatic Classification Plugin, in WGS 84 / UTM Zone 45N. The plugin read the metadata file to check the reflectance scaling, and bands 1–7 were stacked into one image. A 5-4-3 false colour composite (NIR, red, green) was used to inspect the landscape and choose training areas. Histograms of each band and of the whole stack were checked for spread, separation between land cover types and clipping. Six classes were then classified with the Maximum Likelihood method, using training polygons digitised from the composite and local knowledge. Accuracy was assessed with a confusion matrix. Class areas were calculated from pixel counts at 30 m. Separately, NDVI (bands 5 and 4) and the Bare Soil Index (bands 6, 4, 5 and 2) were computed with the raster calculator and reclassified into five classes each, using thresholds from the literature.

The study used a single Landsat 8 OLI Level-2 surface reflectance scene (Path 140, Row 043, product LC08_L2SP_140043_20170428_20200904_02_T1) acquired on 28 April 2017. It has 3% cloud cover, 30 m resolution and GeoTIFF format, and was downloaded from USGS Earth Explorer. The date was chosen to match the LULC reference layers from ISRO-NRSC’s Bhuvan thematic services. Training and validation samples came from visual interpretation of the false colour composite.

Agricultural land dominates at 865.9 km² (42.5%), followed by vegetation at 390.4 km² (19.1%), mostly in the north-western uplands and river corridors. Wasteland covers 320.3 km² (15.7%) and built-up land 306.4 km² (15.0%), clustered around Dhanbad city and the mining townships. Water bodies cover 78.9 km² (3.9%) and mines 77.9 km² (3.8%), with the mines forming a dense band across the central district. The class areas sum to 2,039.8 km², which matches the district’s stated area. The classification reached an overall accuracy of 91.4% and a Kappa of 0.887. The histograms showed clear separation between the visible, NIR and SWIR bands, with water at the lowest reflectance and mined or built surfaces brightest in SWIR. The NDVI and BSI maps are complementary. NDVI shows what remains green and exposes drought and fire-prone zones. BSI shows what is exposed and highlights erosion hotspots and reclamation gaps. Together they give a low-cost basis for restoration, mitigation targeting and land-use planning.

projects.title: Groundwater recharge potential mapping of Pune district using AHP
projects.summary: GIS-based multi-criteria assessment of groundwater recharge potential across Pune district’s 14 sub-districts. Nine thematic layers were weighted with the Analytic Hierarchy Process (consistency ratio 0.02) and combined into a five-class potential map.

meta.v: Pune district, 14 sub-districts
Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) with GIS overlay
9 layers: geology, geomorphology, slope, relief, drainage density, lineament density, soil, rainfall, LULC

sections.t: Pune district lies in the Deccan Trap region of the Western Ghats and plateau, where groundwater recharge varies sharply from the high-rainfall western hills to the drier eastern sub-districts such as Baramati, Indapur and Daund. Recharge depends on many factors at once, including the underlying rock, landforms, slope, drainage, fractures, soil, rainfall and land use. No single map captures it. The project asks where recharge is likely to be best and where it is poor, so that water-conservation and recharge structures can be targeted.

Nine thematic layers were prepared in ArcGIS Pro and reclassified into ranked classes. Steeper slopes, higher relief and higher drainage density were ranked as poor for recharge, and flat terrain, low relief and low drainage density as good. The layers were weighted with AHP. A 9×9 pairwise comparison matrix was built in Excel and normalised, and the priority weights were calculated by both the eigenvector and row-average methods. The two agree closely, which supports the weights. The consistency check gave λmax = 9.23, a consistency index of 0.029 and a consistency ratio of 0.020. The weighted layers were then combined into a groundwater recharge potential raster in five classes, from “poor” to “best groundwater potential”. The project also contains thematic maps for each layer and a sub-district map layout. I am assuming the combination step was a weighted overlay, since the project file only shows the output layer.

The layers are geology (Deccan Trap and related units), geomorphology (landforms such as fluvial, denudational and structural hills), slope, relief, drainage density, lineament density, FAO soil types (for example Vertic Cambisols, Nitisols and Fluvisols), rainfall and land use/land cover (water bodies, built-up, forest, scrub and grassland). Administrative boundaries cover the district and its 14 sub-districts: Junnar, Ambegaon, Shirur, Khed, Mawal, Mulshi, Haveli, Pune City, Daund, Purandhar, Velhe, Bhor, Baramati and Indapur. The sources of the thematic layers aren’t recorded in the files, so add them if you want them shown.

Geology gets the highest weight at 29.0%, followed by geomorphology at 21.9%, slope at 12.2%, relief at 10.3% and drainage density at 9.1%. Soil (4.8%), land cover (4.7%), lineament density (4.2%) and rainfall (3.7%) carry the least. Together, the first five factors account for about 74% of the total weight, so the map is driven mostly by the physical character of the terrain. The consistency ratio of 0.020 is well under the 0.10 limit, so the judgements are acceptably consistent. The final map classes are poor groundwater potential, limited infiltration, moderate infiltration, good infiltration and best groundwater potential. The class areas aren’t in the files I received.

projects.title: Tracking Hurricane Katrina (2005) from ERA5 sea-level pressure
projects.place: Gulf of Mexico and south-east USA
projects.summary: A Python workflow that finds Hurricane Katrina’s centre in six-hourly ERA5 sea-level pressure fields. It builds a track and a pressure time series, and animates the storm as a GIF. The deepest point is 935.8 hPa near the Louisiana coast on 29 August.

meta.v: Hurricane Katrina, August 2005
ERA5 mean sea-level pressure (Copernicus Climate Data Store)
Python, xarray, NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib, Cartopy, imageio

sections.t: Hurricane Katrina formed over the Bahamas in late August 2005, crossed southern Florida, strengthened over the Gulf of Mexico, and made landfall on the Louisiana and Mississippi coast on 29 August. Tracking a cyclone’s centre through time is a basic step in hazard monitoring and early warning. This project shows how far a simple, reproducible workflow can go using only one reanalysis variable, sea-level pressure, without any best-track dataset.

The workflow runs in a Jupyter notebook. The ERA5 download is written as a function, but it is commented out and the NetCDF file was downloaded beforehand. Pressure is converted from pascals to hPa, subset to the study window, and resampled to six-hourly steps. Each field is lightly smoothed with a Gaussian filter, and the grid cell with the lowest pressure is taken as the cyclone centre. The resulting latitude, longitude and minimum pressure are written to a CSV file. The notebook then plots minimum pressure over time, maps the track with Cartopy coastlines and borders, and renders one frame per time step. The frames show the pressure field with the track so far, and they are stitched into an animated GIF at 0.3 seconds per frame.

The input is ERA5 mean sea-level pressure from ECMWF through the Copernicus Climate Data Store (about 25 km grid, hourly or six-hourly). The intended domain is 15–35°N, 100–75°W, covering the Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico and south-east USA. The file holds 68 time steps and the notebook subsets it to 23 August to 1 September 2005. The outputs are a 36-row CSV of time, latitude, longitude and pressure, 36 PNG frames, and the GIF.

The pressure series shows the storm deepening clearly. Pressure is about 1,003 hPa on 25 August and falls through the Gulf to about 987 hPa on 27 August and 952 hPa on 28 August. It bottoms out at 935.8 hPa on 29 August at 12:00 UTC near 29.25°N, 89.5°W, which matches Katrina’s landfall near the mouth of the Mississippi. The pressure then rises quickly as the storm moves inland, passing 978 hPa on 30 August and 1,000 hPa by that evening. ERA5 smooths intense storms, so its minimum is shallower than the roughly 902–920 hPa observed in Katrina. The path through the Gulf and up to landfall looks correct in the animation. The early and late parts of the track are not reliable, as explained below.

tools: xarray, netCDF4, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Matplotlib, Cartopy, imageio, tqdm
ERA5 reanalysis, Copernicus Climate Data Store (cdsapi)

projects.title: How variable is Mumbai’s humidity? A 35-year analysis in R
projects.summary: An R analysis of 35 years of daily relative humidity for Mumbai from NASA POWER. It separates random day-to-day swings, the seasonal monsoon cycle and long-term change, and finds the seasonal cycle explains about 93% of monthly variance.

meta.v: Relative humidity at 2 m (RH2M)
NASA POWER, daily, 1 Jan 1990 to 31 Dec 2024 (12,784 days)
R, RStudio, tidyverse, ggplot2

sections.t: Humidity shapes cloud and rain formation, heat comfort and energy use, and this matters most in humid coastal cities like Mumbai. Climate variability comes in two kinds. Random variability is short-term fluctuation with no repeating pattern, and periodic variability is the repeating seasonal and year-to-year rhythm. Separating them shows how much of what people experience is predictable (the monsoon cycle) and how much is not. The assignment asks how much of Mumbai’s humidity is random, how much is seasonal, and whether the variability is changing over time.

Daily values were cleaned in R, then aggregated to monthly and yearly averages and saved as new CSV files. Three analyses followed. For random variability, a seasonal mean was calculated for each day of the year and subtracted, leaving residuals. These were examined with a histogram, a Q–Q plot, monthly boxplots, ACF and PACF plots, and a rolling 30-day standard deviation. For periodic variability, monthly means with 95% confidence intervals, boxplots, a year-by-month heatmap and a variance decomposition (total variance split into seasonal and residual parts) were produced. For change over time, annual means, year-to-year changes and a trend-versus-residual variance split were calculated.

The data come from NASA POWER, which provides satellite- and model-derived meteorological series. The daily file has three columns (year, day of year and RH2M), with no gaps and values from about 13% to 96%. The monthly file (420 rows) and yearly file (35 rows) were built from it in R.

Humidity has a very strong seasonal rhythm. It is lowest in February–March at about 44–45%, climbs sharply in June and stays near 89–90% through July–September, then falls from October. The seasonal cycle explains 92.9% of monthly variance, leaving 7.1% for anomalies. After removing the seasonal mean, daily humidity still varies by about 8 percentage points. That is much more than the roughly 2-point spread between annual averages. The daily residuals are strongly persistent (lag-1 autocorrelation about 0.8), have slightly heavy tails, and vary more in some seasons than others. Annual mean humidity ranges between 63.6% (2002) and 71.7% (2020). It rose slightly across the period (about +0.5 points per decade), but the trend explains only 7.7% of annual variance and is not statistically significant. The biggest year-to-year jumps were +5 points in 2010 and drops of about 4 points in 2002, 2018 and 2023, so natural year-to-year variation dominates.

projects.title: Cyclone risk to Odisha’s transmission towers
projects.place: Odisha, India · Cyclone Fani (2019) and 10,000 simulated cyclone years
projects.summary: Probabilistic cyclone risk assessment of 41,814 transmission towers in Odisha. It finds about INR 168 crore of expected annual damage and tests whether higher design wind speeds or targeted hardening would pay off, using only free and open-source tools.

meta.v: 41,814 towers, 227 substations, 327 lines
10,000 synthetic years of STORM cyclones (3,387 cyclones within 300 km of Odisha)
Cyclone Fani 2019: 128 damaged towers, median gust 72.9 m/s

sections.t: Cyclones repeatedly damage Odisha’s power network, and the losses are large. The 2019 Fani cyclone caused INR 8,139 crore of damage and loss to the power sector, which is 33.7% of its total INR 24,176 crore, and cut supply to about 4.6 million consumers. In Fani, 128 towers on 132/220 kV lines were damaged and 87 of them collapsed. Rebuilding to the old standard would repeat the risk. The project is part of the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) Odisha power-sector programme. It links to the Sendai Framework (damage to critical infrastructure) and SDG 9.1 (resilient infrastructure). Earlier work gave prioritisation indicators or Fani fragility curves, but no probabilities, loss estimates or cost-benefit. This project adds three things: a design-code comparison on one wind basis, probabilistic losses from 10,000 simulated years, and a cost-benefit test of upgrading design versus hardening existing lines.

The work was organised as six workstreams: a concept note and review, a Fani case study, a design-code gap analysis, probabilistic risk, options and cost-benefit, and a briefing note. The model chains six steps. It starts with STORM synthetic cyclone tracks (3,387 cyclones within 300 km of Odisha) and applies a Holland wind field with translation asymmetry at every tower. Mean wind is then converted to a 3-second gust with WMO TD-1555 cyclone factors. A lognormal fragility curve is fitted on the 128 Fani-damaged towers and used to estimate tower and line failures, with a Monte Carlo simulation of network outage. Finally, expected and return-period losses are calculated, along with the 30-year NPV and benefit-cost ratio for each option. The codes IS 875 and IS 802 were compared on a common basis by converting design winds into 3-second gusts and 10-minute means. Two options were assessed. In option (a), new towers in the 0–60 km coastal band are built for 20% higher wind at 20% extra cost. In option (b), the 10 riskiest lines, about 3,300 towers, are retrofitted at INR 35 lakh per tower.

The network of 41,814 towers, 227 substations and 327 lines comes from OpenStreetMap, via Raj et al. Damage records for the 128 towers damaged in Fani come from OPTCL, obtained through RTI. The hazard data are STORM’s 10,000 synthetic years, with IBTrACS 1980–2025 used for comparison. Design codes are IS 875 (1987, 2015), IS 802 (1995) and the OPTCL specification. Cost and loss figures come from the Fani DLNA, CDRI and the World Bank Lifelines work, and Natural Earth, GADM and Meteostat supply supporting data.

Damaged towers in Fani saw a median modelled gust of 72.9 m/s (262 km/h). 96% were above the IS 875 basic wind speed of 50 m/s, and 84% were above OPTCL’s design wind of 39.3 m/s (10-minute). Four lines near Puri account for 87% of the damage. The fitted fragility median of 81.9 m/s agrees with an independent result by Raj et al. (81.2 m/s), and Fani was roughly a 1-in-80-year wind for those towers. A cyclone passes within 300 km about once every three years, and hazard is highest on the central coast, with a 50-year gust of 62 m/s from Puri to Kendrapara and a 100-year gust of 78 m/s at Puri.

IS 802 converts gusts with a factor of 1.375, while the WMO cyclone factor over land is 1.66, a 21% difference in wind speed and 46% in wind load. The larger issue is how fast cyclone winds grow with return period. For Puri, the hazard rises 77% from the 50-year to the 500-year wind, while IS 802 rises only 28%. As a result, 96–100% of study towers exceed the reliability level 2 and 3 design winds.

Expected annual damage is INR 168 crore, of which about INR 100 crore (59%) is outage cost and INR 68 crore is repairs. The 25-year loss is INR 744 crore, the 50-year loss INR 2,894 crore and the 100-year loss INR 5,516 crore, while the 10-year loss is only about INR 3 crore, so the risk comes from rare severe cyclones. Of the 500 highest-risk towers, 370–450 are in Puri district, about 75% are on 132 kV lines, and 76–89% are within 20 km of the coast.

Neither option pays at today’s assumptions. Raising design wind gives a benefit-cost ratio of 0.49 (0.22 on repairs alone, NPV −INR 190 crore), and hardening the top corridors gives 0.17 (0.10 on repairs alone, NPV −INR 893 crore). Option (a) breaks even if the extra cost per new tower is 10% or less, or if unserved energy is valued at INR 290/kWh or more. A tower would need about a 4.5% yearly damage chance before a retrofit pays on repairs, but today’s highest is under 1%.

The recommendations are to use cyclone-specific return-period scaling, or adopt the IS 875:2015 factor in IS 802, and to use WMO cyclone gust factors. New coastal lines in the 0–60 km band should be designed for higher wind, starting with Puri to Kendrapara. Existing lines should be retrofitted only where outages hit hospitals, ports, water supply or industry. The data gaps should be closed with Phailin damage records, anemometers at coastal substations, and an agreed value of lost load. The code return-period gap and the near break-even case for higher design wind on new coastal lines hold across assumptions, but absolute tower counts do not.

Fragility comes from a single cyclone, so it transfers poorly to others. Exposure uses a distance-to-coast rule, and STORM represents the present climate and under-represents the south coast. Today’s network is used for past cyclones, and the IS 875:2015, IS 802:2015 and CEA 2022 values are still to be verified.

projects.title: Grid stress test for Nagpur: storms, heat and the services that depend on power
projects.summary: Open-source stress test of a power grid around Nagpur under windstorms and future heat. It follows the failures into hospitals and water supply, then sizes solar-plus-battery backup. Extreme storms cost about 515 critical service-hours per event, and heat adds up to 14 failing N-1 contingencies by 2050.

meta.v: IEEE 118-bus test grid placed synthetically around Nagpur
500 Monte Carlo runs, severe (50 m/s) and extreme (55 m/s) gusts
445 hospitals (59 major, 11,800 beds), 14 water nodes, 2.71 million people

sections.t: Hospitals, water pumping and telecom all stop when the grid stops. Heatwaves are rising across India, and storms can cause multi-day outages, as in the 2012 blackout and Cyclone Fani in 2019. Heat adds a second problem: hot air cools overhead conductors less, so lines carry less current just when demand peaks. The project asks how future heat and hazard outages stress a power grid, and how far the failures spread into health and water services. It addresses four gaps in the literature. Heat derating is rarely carried through to N-1 contingency performance for Indian climate data. Hazard studies report megawatts lost, not hospital or water service lost. Rooftop PV is studied for hosting capacity or for backup, seldom both on one feeder. Backup is sized for assumed 24 h or 72 h outages rather than hazard-informed ones. The work links to the Sendai Framework, SDG 7.1, 9.1 and 3, and the Paris Agreement’s adaptation and mitigation co-benefits.

The work is one open workflow of five linked modules, each feeding the next. In the contingency module, all 186 lines and transformers of the IEEE 118-bus network were removed one at a time with a full AC power flow. A linear-programming DC optimal power flow with sheddable loads then found which outages actually lose load, and this was checked against pandapower. Storm N-k scenarios used a Gaussian gust footprint along a swept storm track, lognormal tower fragility based on the IS 875 basic wind speed (44 m/s), and 500 Monte Carlo runs with three repair crews. A feeder module put rooftop PV on a CIGRE medium-voltage feeder to find hosting capacity, using NASA POWER solar data and pvlib. The heat module implemented the IEEE 738 steady-state heat balance from scratch for an ACSR Zebra conductor at 75 °C, validated against the standard’s Drake example (1,025 A). It used the 99th-percentile March–June hot days from 30 NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 models (baseline 1985–2014 versus 2041–2070, SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5), then derated every overhead line and reran the N-1 analysis. The cascade module built a directed NetworkX graph from grid buses to water nodes to hospitals and simulated it hour by hour with water reservoirs (8 h), hospital tanks (12 h) and diesel backup (24 h for major hospitals, 4 h for small ones). The mitigation module sized solar-plus-battery backup against the modelled outage durations by starting outages at every March–June hour from 2005 to 2024 and choosing the least-cost system with at least 95% survival.

The hazard and network inputs are the IEEE 118-bus and CIGRE medium-voltage test networks, with the grid placed synthetically around Nagpur (21.15°N, 79.09°E). Weather and climate data come from NASA POWER hourly data and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 through Google Earth Engine. Hospitals and water infrastructure come from OpenStreetMap, and population (2.71 million people) from WorldPop 2020. The locations and population are real, but the mapping of facilities to grid buses is synthetic. Fragility, cost and load parameters are illustrative.

Many single outages overload lines, but few lose load. Of 186 single outages, 40 violate limits (31 thermal, 12 voltage), and only 4 force load shedding after generators are re-dispatched. The worst case is transformer T12, which isolates a sub-area and loses 84 MW. Storms are far more damaging because they break many nearby lines at once. A severe storm (50 m/s) fails about 7 lines on average, with 13 MW mean load at risk and about 30 hours to restore. An extreme storm (55 m/s) fails about 26 lines, puts 138 MW at risk on average (237 MW at most), and takes about 53 hours to restore, with roughly 4,700 MWh of unserved energy per event.

Rooftop PV can reach about 2.2 times peak load (about 11 MW) on the feeder before limits are hit, with voltage rise binding first. All 12 feeder-section outages can be restored with tie switches. PV peaks at noon while demand peaks at 20:00, so storage is needed.

Heat raises the design hot-day temperature from 46.4 °C by 1.7 °C (SSP2-4.5) or 2.6 °C (SSP5-8.5). This cuts line capacity by a median of 3.5% and 6.1%, and by 9.8% in a hotter model. N-1 violations rise from 40 to 46 for the median SSP5-8.5 model, 52 for a hot model, and 54 when heat-driven demand growth is added. Total overload more than doubles. Load at risk barely moves (84 to 94 MW) because re-dispatch absorbs the overloads, so heat first erodes the security margin.

In the service cascade, storms drive the losses, not single outages. An extreme storm costs about 515 critical service-hours per event on average, with up to 27 hospitals affected, compared with about 78 for a severe storm, 1 for a single outage and 0.5 for an outage during a heat period. Extending diesel at small hospitals from 4 h to 24 h cuts losses by 67%. About 6% of hospital-hours are lost through water failure, and water storage and diesel at major hospitals change results by less than 10%.

Preliminary backup results use an earlier facility set. A hospital PV-plus-battery system costs about ₹4.2 crore a year gross and ₹0.6 crore after energy savings, and avoids about 66 critical service-hours per storm event. Pumping stations cost about 12 times more per service-hour avoided.

The recommendations are to plan with climate-adjusted line ratings, harden storm-exposed corridors and pre-position repair crews, extend backup duration at small hospitals first, and solarise hospitals as a no-regret Build Back Better step. The next steps are real MSEDCL/MSETCL network data, a telecom layer, and annual event probabilities.

The study uses test networks, not Nagpur’s real grid, and the facility-to-bus mapping is synthetic. The DC-OPF assumes corrective re-dispatch, and the fragility, cost and load parameters are illustrative. Event probabilities aren’t included, so the results are scenario losses, not annual risk.

projects.title: Observed extreme fire weather in Southern Europe, 1950–2025: trends, drivers and what the Fire Weather Index misses
projects.summary: 76-year analysis of fire weather across Southern Europe, built from ERA5 and checked against the official Copernicus index. Extreme fire weather has risen about 2–3 times faster since 1979, and drier air is the main driver. Three deadly fires (Portugal 2017, Greece 2021) show that the Fire Weather Index misses unstable, dry air aloft.

meta.v: ERA5 daily at 12 UTC, 1950–2025, about 3,250 burnable cells (0.25°)
r = 0.98 against Copernicus FWI in all 8 test years
Hot, dry and windy days occur 3.6–5.3× more often than by chance

sections.t: The Fire Weather Index (FWI) is the standard measure of dangerous fire conditions, but it uses only surface weather. Some of the deadliest fires in Southern Europe, such as Pedrógão Grande (Portugal, June 2017), central and northern Portugal (October 2017) and Greece (August 2021), were not always high-FWI fires. Unstable, dry air aloft can let a fire build its own storm clouds, and the FWI cannot see that. The project asks four questions. How have fire-weather intensity, frequency and season length changed since 1950? Which ingredient drives the change: heat, humidity, wind or rain? How rare were the record events compared with the 1950s climate? Was the upper air unusually unstable and dry? The main question is whether climate attribution based only on FWI misses part of the danger.

The work is six steps, each in its own Python notebook. (1) ERA5 surface data was downloaded through Google Earth Engine and upper-air data from Copernicus. (2) FWI was computed daily for the whole year with xclim and checked against the Copernicus FWI. (3) Trends and fire-season length were tested with Mann–Kendall and Theil–Sen methods, with false-discovery-rate control. (4) To find the drivers, the trend of one input at a time was removed, and hot, dry and windy days were counted. (5) The rarity of the record events was estimated with an extreme-value (GEV) model linked to global mean temperature, comparing a 1950s climate with the 2017 climate. (6) Weather patterns aloft were studied with 500 hPa ridges, a blocking index and the Continuous Haines Index, comparing each event year with the other 75 years.

ERA5 daily reanalysis at 12 UTC, 1950–2025, on a 0.25° grid (about 25 km) over 35–46°N and 10°W–30°E, restricted to about 3,250 burnable cells. Surface data comes from Google Earth Engine and upper-air data from the Copernicus data stores. The FWI was validated against the Copernicus FWI for 8 test years: daily correlation is r = 0.98 and the mean bias is −0.3 to −1.1, because the inputs are taken at 12 UTC rather than local noon.

Fire-weather extremes have risen since 1979. The 95th-percentile FWI rises by +2.12 per decade (+0.87 over 1950–2025), the mean FWI by +1.03 per decade, and extreme days by +2.7 per decade. About 80% of grid cells show a significant rise in the 95th-percentile FWI since 1979. The fire season now starts earlier and lasts longer: 2.8 days longer per decade with a fixed threshold (FWI ≥ 21.3) and 5.5 days longer with a relative threshold (each cell’s 75th percentile). The start moves 3–4 days earlier per decade, while the end barely moves.

Drier air drives the rise, ahead of heat. Of the +2.1 per decade rise in 95th-percentile FWI since 1979, humidity adds 1.1 and temperature 0.6, and wind and rain add almost nothing. In 99.7% of the cells where FWI rose, the air is drying. Hot, dry and windy days now coincide 3.6–5.3 times more often than expected by chance. Hot and dry days travel together, so compound days rise mainly because each type is becoming more common. Hot and dry days average 7.8 per season and are rising by 2.7 days per decade since 1979.

For the record events, the Pedrógão FWI of 38.7 was a 1-in-2-year value today (5.5 years in the 1950s climate), yet warming made it 2.7 times more likely (95% CI 1.5–5.6, p = 0.004). October 2017 (FWI 62.1) was about a 1-in-80-year event, with a probability ratio of 2.7 that is not significant (p = 0.13). Greece in August 2021 (FWI 59.3) was about 1-in-13 years, ratio 1.8, also not significant (p = 0.37).

Instability aloft was extreme in all three events. The Continuous Haines Index peaked at 10.2 in Portugal in June 2017 (normal top 7.4), 9.4 in October 2017 (6.6) and 12.4 in Greece in August 2021 (8.4). For Greece, a subtropical ridge built over the central Mediterranean during 7–10 August. Pedrógão therefore had an ordinary FWI but record instability aloft.

Next steps are to add more events (Attica 2018, Evros and Rhodes 2023), to test whether warming has made extreme instability aloft more likely, and to compare the observed extremes with climate-model experiments.

ERA5 uses fewer observations before 1979, and early-1950s values look unusually high, so every trend is also reported from 1979. Inputs at 12 UTC cause a small negative bias against the official FWI. Only three events were analysed, and two of the three climate signals are not statistically significant.

projects.title: Unprecedented fire weather in India: how bad can pre-monsoon fire weather get, today and at 1.5, 2 and 3 °C of warming?
projects.place: Central India (Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh) and Uttarakhand
projects.summary: UNSEEN analysis that pools 170 climate-model simulations into about 3,400 plausible fire seasons per warming level. In Central India a season 9% beyond the observed record is already plausible today, and the odds of a record season rise from 1-in-56 to 1-in-7 years at +3 °C. Uttarakhand shows no robust warming signal but a large hidden tail.

meta.v: UNSEEN: 170 simulations from 4 CMIP6 large ensembles, about 3,400 seasons per warming level
Central India annual-max FWI 84.0 (2010)
Up to 20× more likely once-in-100-year count of extreme days at +3 °C

sections.t: Planners need the plausible worst case and its odds, not only the worst year so far. The observed record is about 48 years of reliable data (ERA5-Land, 1979–2026), far too short to estimate a 1-in-100-year fire season. Uttarakhand’s 2016, 2021 and 2024 forest-fire seasons showed how fast pre-monsoon fire weather turns dangerous, and Central India’s dry-deciduous forests burn every spring, about 10,000 km² per season in recent years (MODIS). The project asks three questions. What is the worst fire weather plausible in today’s climate, beyond the observed record? How likely is a record-breaking season in any given year? How do these change at 1.5, 2 and 3 °C, and is it heat, dryness or wind? Two contrasting regions were studied: Central India (Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh, plains, peak March–May) and Uttarakhand (Himalayan foothills, peak April–May).

The work uses the UNSEEN method in five steps. (1) Observed FWI was computed from ERA5-Land (1950–2026) via Google Earth Engine, using the same FWI code as for the models. (2) Model FWI was computed for four CMIP6 large ensembles: CanESM5 (50 members), MIROC6 (50), ACCESS-ESM1-5 (40) and MPI-ESM1-2-LR (30). (3) Models were tested for fidelity (mean, standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis) and bias-corrected with a mean–variance correction. (4) Members were pooled by warming level, using 20-year windows where each member reaches 1.3, 1.5, 2 and 3 °C. Comparing at the same global temperature removes most of the spread between models that warm at different rates. (5) Exceedance curves, the probability of a new record and the worst plausible season were calculated, and maps were made in QGIS. FWI (Canadian system) comes from daily maximum temperature, minimum humidity, wind and rain, the standard proxy when models give daily output only.

ERA5-Land 1950–2026 via Google Earth Engine for observations, and daily output from CanESM5, MIROC6, ACCESS-ESM1-5 and MPI-ESM1-2-LR large ensembles for the model side. MODIS burned area (February–June, 2001–2026) was used to check that fire weather tracks real fires. Model grids are 2.5°.

Fire weather tracks fires in Uttarakhand (rank correlation ρ = 0.70 with burned area) but not in Central India (ρ ≈ −0.1), where human ignition dominates. A daily proxy was used instead of true noon FWI and reads 10–14% lower, but year rankings are preserved (rank correlation 0.92–0.96). Raw model biases are large (+6 to +39 FWI units in Central India), but after correction all four models pass all four fidelity tests.

In Central India the observed record is an annual-maximum FWI of 84.0 (2010). The worst plausible season today is 91.4, 9% above the record, and the worst plausible at +3 °C is 105, 25% above it. The yearly chance of beating the 2010 record is 1.8% today, 2.3% at +1.5 °C, 4.1% at +2 °C and 13.4% at +3 °C, which turns a 1-in-56-year record into a 1-in-7-year one. The chance of at least one new record in the next 10 years goes from 16% to 76%. Models disagree at +3 °C, from no change (MPI-ESM1-2-LR) to 24% per year. The risk concentrates over Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and the northern Deccan, while the Himalaya changes little.

Extremes become more persistent, not longer. The once-in-100-year count of extreme days per year becomes up to 20 times more likely at +3 °C (11× in CanESM5). The chance of a record 90-day sustained FWI rises from 1.5% to 9% per year, while the total length of the fire-weather season stays flat.

In Uttarakhand there is no robust warming signal, and models disagree on the sign. The chance of beating the 1989 record stays at about 1.5% per year at every warming level. A large tail is hidden in the short record: the worst plausible season today is 23% above the record, and the record is a 1-in-520-year event by a GEV fit on the short record but 1-in-65 by UNSEEN.

Extreme seasons are hot, dry and, above all, windy. Wind explains 43% of year-to-year FWI variation in Central India (temperature 29%, humidity 21%, rain 7%) and 61% in Uttarakhand (humidity 30%, temperature 5%, rain 4%). In the models, extreme Uttarakhand years come with a deepened surface heat low over the foothills, not a blocking high, and future increases are mainly heat-driven but leave large unexplained residuals (exploratory).

A daily proxy replaces noon values (rankings preserved). The 2.5° model grid leaves Uttarakhand with only about 4 cells. The analysis uses one scenario framing (warming levels) and monthly drivers. FWI is weather only and has no fuels or ignition. Next steps are daily blocking and heatwave diagnostics, higher-resolution or downscaled ensembles for the Himalaya, validation against IMD stations and fire records, and fuel moisture and ignition for fire-impact risk.

projects.title: Biodiversity impact screening of heavy industry in Chandrapur, next to Tadoba
projects.summary: Open-data screening of six heavy-industry sites near the Tadoba-Andhari Tiger Reserve, using Google Earth Engine and the TNFD LEAP approach. The main pressure is land conversion, not forest loss: 221 to 1,509 ha of natural land converted within 10 km of each site versus 0 to 40 ha of forest loss. Five sites score Medium and one Low, and actions are proposed by cluster.

meta.v: 6 plants (3 cement, 1 steel, 1 coal power; one site covers two cement units)
10 plants have binding carbon targets, the 2,920 MW coal station is outside the carbon market, and none are tracked for nature
TNFD LEAP with four tests scored 0–2

sections.t: Chandrapur has two policy worlds in one district. Ten plants (5 cement, 4 steel or ferro-alloy, 1 paper) now have binding carbon targets, while a 2,920 MW coal power station sits outside the carbon market. The same district holds the Tadoba-Andhari Tiger Reserve, a 625 km² core and 1,102 km² buffer linked by corridors to Kawal, Indravati, Nagzira-Navegaon and Pench (NTCA). The plants’ carbon is now regulated, but their effect on nature is not tracked anywhere. This is the third of three connected projects: carbon signals in Indian policy are weak, forest-carbon targets can be met with plantations that do little for biodiversity, and the same plants face carbon rules but no biodiversity rules.

The screening follows the TNFD LEAP approach with open satellite data. Locate: 6 sites with verified coordinates, 5 and 10 km buffers, and Tadoba and forest boundaries. Evaluate: what each industry depends on and how it affects nature. Assess: land cover, forest loss 2015–24, land conversion 2016–25 and surface water. Prepare: a 0–2 score on four tests (proximity to a formal protected area, natural habitat, land loss, water), giving a total of 0–8, followed by actions by cluster.

ESA WorldCover 2021, Hansen Global Forest Change, Google Dynamic World, JRC Surface Water and OpenStreetMap. A data gap was found and fixed: Earth Engine’s protected-area layer holds 7,180 forest compartments for the area but omits Tadoba itself, so Tadoba boundaries were taken from OpenStreetMap instead.

The main pressure is land conversion, not forest loss. Within 10 km, natural land converted to built-up or bare ground in 2016–25 was 1,509 ha at Lloyds Metals (Ghugus), 1,426 ha at ACC Chanda, 1,345 ha at Chandrapur STPS, 523 ha at UltraTech Awarpur, 264 ha at UltraTech Manikgarh I & II and 221 ha at Ambuja Maratha. Forest loss in 2015–24 was only 40 ha at Chandrapur STPS, 1 ha at Lloyds and ACC, and 0 ha elsewhere.

Five sites score Medium and one Low. Chandrapur STPS (17.9 km to mapped Tadoba, 56% natural land within 10 km), Lloyds Metals, ACC Chanda and UltraTech Manikgarh each score 4 of 8. UltraTech Awarpur scores 3, with a Reserve or Protected Forest only 0.1 km away. Ambuja Maratha scores 2 (Low).

The proposed actions are by cluster, not by plant. For the power station, restore ash ponds and closed mine land as grassland, scrub and wetland, keep the forest edge free of new ash land, and report on biodiversity although it sits outside the carbon market. For Ghugus and the Wardha valley, run one shared cumulative-impact study by cement, steel and mining firms and restore mined-out land along the river as habitat and water bodies. For the Korpana cement cluster, rehabilitate exhausted limestone quarries into native habitat and protect forest compartments within 1–2 km of Awarpur and Manikgarh. Two next steps follow: disclose with maps, answering BRSR’s question on ecologically sensitive areas with mapped buffers, and pilot the screening with willing firms through IKI, adding field and species data and turning it into a tool for other districts.

Results should be read as landscape pressure, not as impacts caused by a single plant. Buffers overlap and coal mines are not mapped, so change near a plant cannot be blamed on that plant alone. The Tadoba buffer is not mapped in open data, so the power station is likely closer to protected land than 17.9 km. The screening uses no field or species data.

field.title: Mainstreaming Disaster Risk Reduction in Development Planning: Ahmedabad City
field.summary: A group case study of how Disaster Risk Reduction is, and is not, built into Ahmedabad’s City Development Plan. It profiles the city’s growth, governance, hazards (heatwaves, floods, earthquakes, industrial risk) and vulnerabilities. It reviews measures such as the Heat Action Plan and seismic microzonation, and recommends making DRR an explicit, cross-cutting part of planning.

meta.v: 7.7 million (2023), up from 0.8 million in 1951
House about 34% of residents
India’s first (2013); about 1,100 lives saved 2013–2022

sections.t: Ahmedabad was founded in 1411 on the Sabarmati River and became the “Manchester of the East” through textiles. The mill closures of the 1970s–80s pushed 40,000–50,000 workers into slums. The economy then shifted to pharmaceuticals, chemicals and services, and the old walled city became India’s first UNESCO World Heritage City in 2017. Growth split the city into a residential west and an industrial east. AUDA (est. 1978) governs 1,866 sq km and had prepared 357 Town Planning Schemes by 2020. Developed land grew 37% between 2001 and 2021. Governance is divided between AMC (core services) and AUDA (peri-urban areas), and AMC has no dedicated DRR cell. The main hazards are extreme heat (the 2010 heatwave, about 48.3°C, led to the Heat Action Plan), urban flooding and waterlogging (800–1,000 mm annual rainfall), earthquakes (a legacy of 2001), air pollution, and industrial accident risk around Vatva and Naroda.

This is a desk-based plan review supported by field insight. The topic was scoped with the instructor, then the team reviewed academic, government and institutional sources (DP 2031, HAP, GSDMP, CEPT, UNDRR, World Bank). They also drew on earlier field visits and case discussions on informal settlements. The report was structured around urban context, DRR theory, the planning process, a vulnerability profile, SWOT, best practices and recommendations. The planning process was mapped in seven steps: plan formulation, data collection and mapping, stakeholder consultation, drafting and review, public notification and feedback, approval and implementation, then monitoring and evaluation. Drafts were refined through peer and instructor feedback and cited in APA style.

Ahmedabad faces multiple and interconnected urban hazards. These include extreme heat, monsoon-related flooding and waterlogging, earthquake risk, air pollution and industrial accidents. The 2010 heatwave, during which temperatures reportedly reached approximately 48.3°C, highlighted the city's vulnerability to extreme heat. Annual rainfall of around 800–1,000 mm, combined with inadequate drainage and urban expansion, contributes to recurring waterlogging.

Vulnerability is further shaped by rapid population growth, migration, informal housing, social inequality, inadequate infrastructure and uneven access to essential services. Approximately 34% of the city's residents live in informal settlements, many of which face heightened exposure to environmental hazards and limited access to risk communication and institutional support. These conditions demonstrate that disaster risk is influenced not only by physical hazards but also by the socio-economic and spatial distribution of vulnerabilities.

sections.h: DRR Integration in the City Development Plan
sections.t:
Ahmedabad's City Development Plan addresses urban growth, infrastructure development, environmental resilience and socio-economic equity. However, the assessment identifies that the plan does not contain a dedicated Disaster Risk Reduction chapter. Instead, DRR considerations are implicitly incorporated across different sectoral interventions, including affordable housing, slum rehabilitation, urban mobility, water supply, sanitation, stormwater drainage and environmental management.

Programmes under AMRUT, Smart Cities Mission and PMAY-Urban have contributed to infrastructure development and resilience-related interventions. However, the report highlights a significant gap between these individual initiatives and their integration into statutory planning instruments. Climate-risk assessments and hazard studies are not consistently translated into enforceable land-use regulations, making implementation fragmented and potentially uneven across vulnerable neighbourhoods.

Heat Action Plan: Launched in 2013, it introduced colour-coded heat warnings, adjustments to school and working hours, public cooling centres and cool-roof initiatives. The interventions are estimated to have saved more than 1,100 lives between 2013 and 2022.

Urban Flood Management: The Stormwater Drainage Master Plan (2017–2027) identified 147 chronic waterlogging locations. Measures include pumping stations, detention basins, percolation tanks and improvements to stormwater and sewer networks.

Seismic Risk Reduction: Building regulations were strengthened following the 2001 earthquake. The 2019 Seismic Microzonation Study informs risk-sensitive development regulations, while structural safety assessments have been undertaken for public buildings.

Technology and Monitoring: The Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC) supports real-time monitoring and coordination by integrating information related to flooding, traffic and emergency services.

Environmental Resilience: Green spaces, tree plantation, lake rejuvenation and green buffers contribute to urban environmental management and climate resilience.

Despite progress in urban resilience, the assessment identifies persistent institutional and planning gaps. Non-notified informal settlements, particularly those located on private land or facing legal ambiguities, may remain excluded from housing and slum-upgrading programmes. Communities located near drainage channels and industrial areas continue to face considerable exposure to flooding, fire and environmental health risks.

Hazard-sensitive land-use planning also requires improvement. Findings from the 2019 seismic microzonation study have not been fully translated into compulsory zoning restrictions and clearly defined no-build areas. The report also identifies fragmented monitoring and feedback mechanisms, limited institutional coordination and gaps in healthcare continuity for underserved communities. These challenges highlight the need to move from isolated resilience interventions towards an integrated and enforceable DRR planning framework.

Ahmedabad offers several examples of integrating resilience into urban development. AUDA's Town Planning Schemes facilitate the reservation of land for open spaces and public amenities. The Parivartan Slum Networking Project, involving AMC, Mahila Housing Trust and SAATH, demonstrates an approach to improving basic services and living conditions through in-situ settlement upgrading rather than displacement. The Integrated Command and Control Centre also illustrates the application of technology in real-time monitoring and emergency coordination.

Building on these initiatives, the assessment recommends making DRR an explicit and cross-cutting component of the City Development Plan, incorporating seismic and flood-risk assessments into statutory land-use regulations, strengthening institutional coordination, prioritising vulnerable informal settlements and improving community-based disaster preparedness. A more integrated monitoring and evaluation system is also essential to ensure that resilience measures translate into measurable reductions in urban risk.

field.title: Economics of Disasters and Disaster Finance: Evolution of India's Disaster Financing Framework
field.summary: An individual academic study examining the evolution of disaster financing in India, from colonial-era famine relief mechanisms and the Margin Money scheme to the institutionalisation of CRF, NFCR, NCCF, SDRF and NDRF. The study analyses the changing role of successive Finance Commissions, highlighting the transition from a reactive, relief-centric financing approach towards a comprehensive, risk-informed framework covering mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery.

meta.v: Margin Money scheme introduced by the Second Finance Commission (1957–62)
CRF and NCCF transitioned into SDRF and NDRF under the Thirteenth Finance Commission
Fifteenth Finance Commission proposed a dedicated 20% mitigation allocation
₹1,60,153 crore (State SDRMF) and ₹68,463 crore (National NDRMF)

sections.h: Historical Context and Evolution of Disaster Finance
sections.t:
Disaster financing in India has evolved from colonial-era famine relief arrangements into a structured system of fiscal transfers and dedicated disaster management funds. During the late nineteenth century, repeated famines led to the establishment of Famine Commissions in 1880, 1898 and 1901. The Strachey Commission of 1880 recommended dedicated famine relief funding and standardised relief norms, contributing to the establishment of the Provincial Famine Fund and the Indian Famine Codes of 1883.

Following independence, disaster relief continued to depend largely on state budgets and ad-hoc central assistance. An important institutional development came with the Second Finance Commission (1957–62), which introduced the Margin Money scheme, encouraging states to maintain dedicated contingency reserves for disaster relief. This laid the foundation for a more organised system of disaster financing in India's federal fiscal framework.

sections.h: Finance Commissions IX to XII: Institutionalisation of Relief Financing
sections.t:
The Ninth to Twelfth Finance Commissions progressively strengthened India's disaster relief financing architecture by moving away from the earlier Margin Money arrangement towards dedicated state and national-level funds.

The Ninth Finance Commission (1989–95) recommended the Calamity Relief Fund (CRF), with contributions shared between the Centre and States in a 75:25 ratio. The Tenth Finance Commission (1995–2000) proposed the National Fund for Calamity Relief (NFCR) to provide additional assistance during disasters of rare severity. The Eleventh Finance Commission (2000–05) replaced NFCR with the National Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF), supported through a dedicated tax surcharge. The Twelfth Finance Commission (2005–10) continued these arrangements while expanding the list of eligible disasters to include landslides, avalanches, cloudbursts and pest attacks.

These reforms established more predictable funding arrangements for immediate disaster relief, although mitigation and long-term reconstruction remained largely outside the scope of these funds.

sections.h: Finance Commissions XIII and XIV: Alignment with the Disaster Management Act, 2005
sections.t:
The Thirteenth Finance Commission (2010–15) marked an important institutional transition by aligning disaster financing arrangements with the Disaster Management Act, 2005. The existing Calamity Relief Funds were restructured into State Disaster Response Funds (SDRFs), while the National Calamity Contingency Fund was replaced by the National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF).

The Commission also permitted states to utilise up to 10% of their SDRF allocation for certain local disasters not included in the nationally notified disaster list. Capacity-building grants and support for NDRF equipment inventory were introduced, although dedicated mitigation funding remained unprovided.

The Fourteenth Finance Commission (2015–20) largely continued the existing response financing architecture, recommended changes to fund-sharing arrangements and expanded the eligible disaster list to include cold waves and frost. However, concerns regarding vulnerability-based fund allocation and dedicated mitigation financing remained unresolved.

sections.h: Fifteenth Finance Commission: A Paradigm Shift in Disaster Financing
sections.t:
The Fifteenth Finance Commission (2021–26) introduced a significant shift in India's disaster financing approach by extending financial support beyond immediate relief towards mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery.

One of its major recommendations was the establishment of National and State Disaster Mitigation Funds (NDMF and SDMF). It also proposed an integrated Disaster Risk Management Fund architecture, with 80% of allocations directed towards relief, reconstruction and capacity building and 20% exclusively earmarked for mitigation.

The framework recognised the importance of investing in community-level risk reduction, including drainage improvements, embankment strengthening, retrofitting critical infrastructure, early warning systems, training and awareness programmes. This represented a move towards financing disaster risk reduction before disasters occur rather than concentrating resources primarily on post-disaster response.

sections.h: Risk-Based Allocation and Disaster Financing Architecture
sections.t:
A major innovation under the Fifteenth Finance Commission was the introduction of a risk-informed approach to allocating disaster management funds. Earlier allocations were largely based on historical disaster expenditure, which could disadvantage states with high vulnerability but limited financial capacity.

The revised allocation methodology incorporated multiple indicators: 50% weightage to past expenditure, 15% to geographical area, 15% to population and 20% to the Disaster Risk Index. The Disaster Risk Index itself incorporated hazard exposure and vulnerability, with 70% weightage to hazard exposure and 30% to vulnerability.

For the 2021–26 period, the report identifies allocations of ₹1,60,153 crore for State Disaster Risk Management Funds and ₹68,463 crore for the National Disaster Risk Management Fund. The Commission also highlighted alternative financing mechanisms, including CSR contributions, crowdfunding, disaster bonds and international credit.

The evolution of disaster finance in India demonstrates a gradual transition from ad-hoc relief expenditure towards a more institutionalised, proactive and risk-informed financing framework. Successive Finance Commissions have progressively expanded the scope of funding, strengthened Centre–State financial arrangements and recognised the importance of disaster preparedness and mitigation.

The Fifteenth Finance Commission represents a major step towards integrating disaster risk reduction into public finance and development planning. However, the effectiveness of this framework depends on the timely operationalisation of mitigation funds, improved institutional coordination, transparent resource utilisation and effective monitoring of funded interventions.

The study highlights the need to strengthen financial preparedness, incorporate hazard and vulnerability indicators into resource allocation, and diversify financing sources to support long-term disaster resilience.

field.title: Heatwaves and Drought in Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan: Understanding Climate Vulnerability and Development Challenges
field.summary: A comparative study examining the interconnected impacts of heatwaves and droughts in Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan through the lens of climate vulnerability and development. The study explores the influence of climate change, groundwater depletion, land-use transformation, agricultural practices and urbanisation on disaster risk. It further examines socio-economic inequalities, landholding patterns and differential vulnerability among marginalised communities, supported by spatial assessments of heat risk, land surface temperature and precipitation variability. The report concludes with recommendations for climate-resilient agriculture, sustainable water management, improved Heat Action Plans and inclusive disaster preparedness.

meta.v: Rajasthan recorded 26 heatwave days in 2022, according to the study
Rajasthan extracts approximately 145% of its annual renewable groundwater resources
Western Rajasthan experiences rainfall variability exceeding 70% (Coefficient of Variation)

sections.t:
The 2022 heatwave and drought conditions in Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan highlight the interconnected relationship between climate extremes and developmental vulnerabilities. Both states experience recurring extreme temperatures, irregular monsoon patterns and increasing water stress, with particularly severe impacts in Western Rajasthan and the Bundelkhand region of Uttar Pradesh.

The report examines how natural hazards interact with socio-economic and infrastructural conditions to shape disaster vulnerability. Rapid urbanisation, deforestation, groundwater extraction and water-intensive agricultural practices have intensified environmental stress. These challenges are further compounded by poverty, inadequate healthcare, unequal access to resources and limited adaptive capacity.

The study adopts a political economy perspective to understand how historical patterns of land ownership, caste structures, agricultural policies and governance arrangements influence the distribution of climate risks across different population groups.

The study adopts a comparative and spatial assessment approach to examine the relationship between climate hazards and socio-economic vulnerability in Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan.

The assessment brings together state-level developmental indicators, temperature trend visualisations, peak electricity demand analysis, land surface temperature (LST) mapping and precipitation variability assessments. It examines the geographical distribution of heat exposure alongside socio-economic vulnerability to identify regions experiencing overlapping climate and developmental risks.

The report also analyses agricultural dependence, groundwater extraction, land-use changes, urbanisation and infrastructure disparities. Policy and institutional assessments are complemented by a case study of Ahmedabad's Heat Action Plan to understand practical approaches to heatwave preparedness, early warning systems and urban adaptation.

sections.h: Natural and Anthropogenic Drivers of Climate Risk
sections.t:
The report identifies several interconnected natural and human-induced factors contributing to heatwave and drought vulnerability.

Climate change and rising temperatures, combined with increasingly erratic monsoon rainfall, contribute to prolonged dry periods and water scarcity. Deforestation, land degradation and expanding urban settlements further intensify heat exposure by reducing vegetation cover and increasing surface temperatures.

Unregulated groundwater extraction, particularly in Rajasthan and Western Uttar Pradesh, has intensified water stress. Water-intensive agricultural practices, including sugarcane cultivation in Uttar Pradesh and cotton cultivation in Rajasthan, place additional pressure on groundwater resources.

Rapid urbanisation in cities such as Jaipur, Lucknow, Kanpur and Jodhpur has also intensified Urban Heat Island effects through increasing built-up surfaces, reduced green spaces and inadequate climate-sensitive planning.

Heatwaves and droughts do not affect all population groups equally. The study highlights how socio-economic inequalities, particularly landholding disparities, caste-based exclusion and dependence on climate-sensitive livelihoods, influence vulnerability.

Small and marginal farmers, landless agricultural labourers, construction workers, street vendors and migrant communities face disproportionate exposure because of their dependence on outdoor work and limited financial capacity to cope with extreme weather.

Women experience additional vulnerabilities through agricultural dependence, household responsibilities and increased time spent collecting water during drought conditions. Limited access to irrigation, agricultural credit and productive resources further compounds these challenges.

The health and economic consequences include heat-related illness, declining agricultural productivity, income losses, food insecurity, climate-induced migration and increasing pressure on urban infrastructure.

sections.h: Spatial Assessment of Heat Risk and Vulnerability
sections.t:
The report presents comparative spatial assessments of heat exposure, land surface temperature and socio-economic vulnerability across the two states.

In Rajasthan, Western districts such as Jaisalmer, Barmer and Bikaner exhibit high heat exposure alongside significant socio-economic vulnerabilities associated with water scarcity, inadequate infrastructure and arid conditions. The southern and north-eastern regions generally show comparatively lower heat exposure.

In Uttar Pradesh, Bundelkhand emerges as a major area of overlapping heat exposure and socio-economic vulnerability, increasing its susceptibility to drought, agricultural losses and livelihood distress. Purvanchal exhibits considerable socio-economic vulnerability associated with weaker healthcare access and lower adaptive capacity, despite comparatively lower heat exposure.

The report also examines precipitation variability using the Coefficient of Variation (CV). Western Rajasthan exhibits rainfall variability exceeding 70%, while Bundelkhand and eastern Rajasthan experience approximately 40–60% variability. Eastern Uttar Pradesh shows comparatively lower variability of approximately 20–30%.

These spatial patterns highlight the importance of combining hazard exposure with socio-economic vulnerability when identifying priority areas for climate adaptation.

The report examines climate adaptation and disaster risk reduction measures through the five priorities of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction.

An important case study is Ahmedabad's Heat Action Plan, which demonstrates the role of early warning systems, health-sector preparedness, public awareness, cooling infrastructure and institutional coordination in reducing heat-related risks.

The report also discusses the Heat Action Plan frameworks of Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan, heatwave advisories, district-level preparedness and water conservation initiatives.

Key mitigation approaches include climate-resilient agriculture, drought-resistant crops, micro-irrigation, groundwater recharge, urban greening, reflective roofs, cooling shelters and the revival of traditional water conservation systems such as Johads, Baolis and Stepwells.

sections.h: Policy Gaps and Strengthening Climate Resilience
sections.t:
The assessment identifies significant gaps in climate resilience, particularly the limited coverage of Heat Action Plans in rural areas, inadequate district-level preparedness, weak last-mile delivery of early warnings and insufficient regulation of groundwater extraction.

Traditional water conservation systems, including Johads and Stepwells, have not been revived at the required scale. Inadequate rainwater harvesting provisions and limited institutional capacity further constrain sustainable water management.

To address these challenges, the report recommends strengthening four interconnected areas:
1. Climate-resilient agriculture: Promote drought-resistant crops, agricultural diversification, micro-irrigation, crop insurance and improved access to agricultural credit.
2. Urban climate resilience: Expand green infrastructure, improve heat-sensitive housing and strengthen urban heatwave prevention measures.
3. Disaster preparedness: Extend Heat Action Plans to rural regions, improve early warning systems and strengthen local disaster response capacity.
4. Water management: Regulate groundwater extraction, promote water-efficient agriculture and restore traditional water harvesting systems.
The overarching recommendation is to shift from reactive relief-oriented approaches towards inclusive, proactive climate adaptation that integrates disaster risk reduction with sustainable development and social equity.
